Textbook page 531

Chapter roadmap

This introductory page sets out the questions addressed throughout Chapter 24. The main theme is the distinction between fluid volume, fluid concentration, and electrolyte composition.

Fluid volume

How much extracellular fluid is present? Too little produces volume deficit; excess produces volume expansion.

Fluid concentration

How concentrated is the water-solute mixture? Disorders include hyponatremia and hypernatremia.

Fluid distribution

Why does water move into cells, out of cells, or into interstitial spaces?

Electrolyte imbalances

What happens when potassium, calcium, magnesium or phosphate becomes too low or too high?

Study takeaway: Volume and concentration are different concepts. A patient can have an abnormality of either one or both.

Page 531 contains the chapter's key questions and outline rather than detailed mechanisms.

Complete chapter learning checklist

The chapter introduction identifies key questions to answer as you study later sections. Keep this checklist handy; page 531 gives the outline, not full explanations.

  • Recognize factors interfering with fluid intake and thirst.
  • Compare plasma and interstitial fluid composition, especially proteins.
  • Explain capillary filtration versus cellular osmosis.
  • Distinguish ordinary and abnormal fluid loss routes.
  • Identify causes and findings of extracellular volume deficit and excess.
  • Differentiate hyponatremia and hypernatremia and their associated water shifts.
  • Understand the capillary mechanisms producing edema.
  • Recognize how electrolyte intake, absorption, distribution and excretion become abnormal.
  • Identify clinical effects of too little or too much K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and phosphate.
Exam direction: Distinguish isotonic saline-volume disorders from water-concentration disorders. They can occur independently or together.
Textbook page 532

Body fluid compartments

Fluid lubricates tissues, dissolves substances needed for metabolism, transports materials and assists temperature regulation.

How total body fluid is distributed in most adults
Exception: infants initially have a greater proportion of extracellular water.

What's in the extracellular compartment?

Interstitial fluid (between cells), vascular fluid (plasma), fluid in connective tissue/bone, and transcellular fluids such as synovial fluid and CSF.

Different fluids contain different electrolytes

Inside cells (ICF)Outside cells (ECF)
Rich in potassium (K⁺)Rich in sodium (Na⁺)
Rich in magnesium (Mg²⁺)Rich in chloride (Cl⁻)
Phosphates and proteinsRich in bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)
Exam distinction: Plasma has considerably more protein than interstitial fluid. The compartments differ in composition, but their total particle concentrations are normally approximately equal.

Total body water depends on age and body fat

Full-term newborn~75% of body weight
Adult man~60%
Adult woman~50%
Older man~50%
Older womanLess than 50%

More adipose tissue generally means a lower proportion of body weight is water. The textbook's 70-kg adult man example has approximately 42 L total body water, comprising 25 L intracellular and 17 L extracellular water.

The four components of fluid homeostasis

Intake→Absorption→Distribution→Excretion

Abnormal fluid losses may also occur. Increased extracellular osmolality is one stimulus for thirst, with further details on the next page.

Original textbook figure — Fig. 24.1

From Banasik, Pathophysiology, 7th ed., printed p. 532. This is the original illustration showing capillary filtration and osmosis between fluid compartments.

Additional textbook details — page 532

What counts as body fluid?

Body fluid is water plus its dissolved particles. It travels in arteries, veins and lymphatic vessels; is secreted into joint cavities, cerebral ventricles and the gastrointestinal lumen; and surrounds and permeates body cells. It lubricates, enables metabolism, carries oxygen, nutrients, signals and waste, and helps control body temperature.

Compartment-specific composition

ICF is relatively rich in K⁺, Mg²⁺, inorganic and organic phosphates, and proteins, but relatively low in Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Plasma and interstitial ECF are rich in Na⁺, Cl⁻ and bicarbonate. Plasma contains far more protein than interstitial fluid. Transcellular fluids are generally secreted by epithelial cells and have function-dependent compositions. Despite their differing ion mixtures, fluid compartments normally have approximately equal total particle concentrations.

The textbook's 70-kg example

LocationApproximate water volume
Intracellular25 L
Plasma3 L
Interstitial and lymph8 L
Dense connective tissue and bone5 L
Transcellular1 L
Total42 L

One litre of water weighs about 1 kg. Preterm infants contain an even greater proportion of body water than full-term newborns. The proportion falls with aging and increasing body fat; older women typically have less than 50% total body water by weight.

Fluid intake and the homeostasis cycle

Fluid enters through drinks, water in food and small amounts of metabolic water. Intake, absorption, distribution and excretion work together; unusual losses may disrupt the balance. Drinking reflects habit, social factors and thirst. Increased extracellular osmolality begins an osmoreceptor-driven thirst response, discussed further on page 533.

Textbook page 533

Thirst and fluid distribution

Why do you become thirsty?

ECF becomes concentrated→Hypothalamic osmoreceptors→Thirst→Drink water

Other thirst triggers include reduced circulating volume (baroreceptor and angiotensin II pathways) and dry mucous membranes. Osmoreceptor-related thirst is diminished in older adults.

Filtration across capillaries

Water movement between vascular plasma and interstitial fluid reflects the balance of four forces.

Blue arrow: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes outward. Green arrow: plasma protein oncotic pressure pulls inward.
ForceTends to move water
Capillary hydrostatic pressureOut of capillary
Interstitial colloid osmotic pressureOut of capillary
Plasma colloid osmotic pressureInto capillary
Interstitial hydrostatic pressureInto capillary (in the textbook model)
Key contrast: Plasma ↔ interstitial distribution is governed by filtration forces; interstitial ↔ intracellular distribution is governed by osmosis.

Absorption

Fluid taken in through the gastrointestinal tract must be absorbed to enter the vascular compartment. Absorption of electrolytes and other particles creates osmotic forces that help water absorption.

Additional textbook details — page 533

Thirst and clinical risk

Thirst can be triggered by raised extracellular osmolality (osmoreceptors), reduced circulating blood volume (baroreceptors and angiotensin II), and dry oral mucosa. Osmoreceptor-mediated thirst becomes less responsive with aging, increasing the risk of inadequate intake in older adults.

Additional fluid entry routes and absorption

Clinical fluids may be given intravenously, through feeding or drainage tubes into the GI tract or other cavities, subcutaneously, into bone marrow, or rectally (e.g., enema); near-drowning can cause fluid entry into the lungs. Fluids that are not introduced intravenously must be absorbed before reaching the vascular space. In the GI tract, solute and electrolyte absorption helps generate the osmotic forces driving water absorption. Patients who cannot independently control drinking or whose intake is managed medically are vulnerable to imbalance.

All four capillary filtration forces

ForceFavours movement
Capillary hydrostatic pressureFrom capillary → interstitium (outward push)
Interstitial colloid osmotic pressureFrom capillary → interstitium (protein-related pull)
Plasma colloid osmotic pressureFrom interstitium → capillary (plasma protein pull)
Interstitial hydrostatic pressureFrom interstitium → capillary (pressure from outside, in the simplified textbook model)

At any given point, the net balance of opposing pressures determines the direction and amount of filtration. Figure 24.1 (page 532) diagrams filtration across the capillary wall versus osmosis across cell membranes.

Exam trap: Plasma colloid osmotic pressure pulls toward the blood, not toward the tissue. Capillary hydrostatic pressure generally pushes outward.

Age-related body water and the chapter figures

Figure 24.2 shows that the proportion of body weight that is water generally decreases from premature infants to older adults. Figure 24.3 summarizes the fluid homeostasis loop: intake → absorption → distribution → excretion, with additional abnormal losses.

Textbook page 534

Osmosis — try the interactive model

Cell membranes have aquaporins that allow water to cross readily, while many electrolytes require transport proteins. When the effective solute concentration differs, water moves by osmosis toward the more concentrated compartment.

High ECF osmolality → water leaves the cell → cell shrinks
Tap the opposite condition. Watch the cell expand or shrink and the water-flow arrows reverse.
Remember: Water travels toward the compartment with higher effective osmolality. High extracellular concentration shrinks cells; low extracellular concentration swells cells.

Normal and abnormal fluid losses

Fluid normally leaves via urine, skin, lungs and feces. Abnormal routes include vomiting, hemorrhage, wound/fistula drainage, GI tubes and paracentesis. Under normal circumstances the kidney is the largest outlet.

The three fluid-regulating hormones

Tap a hormone below to see how it changes renal water handling.

Free-water retention
Sodium + water retention
Sodium + water excretion
ADH · Antidiuretic hormone
High osmolality / low volume→More free-water reabsorption
Relative urine water output
Small volume of concentrated urine; body fluids diluted
HormoneRelease / triggerMain action
ADHSynthesized in hypothalamus; released from posterior pituitary in response to high osmolality, low blood volume, pain, nausea and stressRenal reabsorption of water; lower urine volume
AldosteroneAdrenal cortex; stimulated by angiotensin II and raised plasma K⁺Renal reabsorption of sodium and water; ECF expansion
ANP / BNPANP: atrial stretch; BNP: increased ventricular stretch/pressureRenal sodium and water excretion
Exam memory: ADH is the free-water hormone. Aldosterone is the salt-water hormone. Natriuretic peptides counter fluid overload by promoting sodium and water excretion.

Additional textbook details — page 534

Osmosis and semipermeable membranes

Aquaporins allow water to pass through cell membranes, while most electrolytes require specific channels or carriers. When osmolality is higher outside a cell, water leaves and the cell shrinks; when osmolality is lower outside, water enters and the cell swells. Osmotic movement tends to equalize effective particle concentrations. Distribution involving transcellular spaces also depends on epithelial secretion.

Visible and insensible losses

Fluid is lost in urine, feces, visible sweat, continuous insensible skin perspiration, and exhaled water vapour. Urine is normally the largest route. Diarrhea can greatly increase fecal water loss. Abnormal routes include vomiting, hemorrhage, GI suction, fistulas, wound drainage, paracentesis and other drainage procedures.

ADH — source, triggers and renal action

ADH is synthesized in the hypothalamic supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released by the posterior pituitary. High ECF osmolality, low circulating blood volume, pain, nausea and physical or psychological stress increase ADH release. ADH raises water reabsorption in the distal nephron and collecting ducts: urine volume falls and becomes concentrated, while retained water tends to dilute body fluids. Low osmolality and ethanol decrease ADH release, favouring large volumes of dilute urine.

Aldosterone — sodium and water conservation

The adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone in response especially to angiotensin II (including during low circulating volume) and high plasma K⁺. Renal sodium reabsorption increases and water is retained, expanding extracellular volume. It is a salt-and-water regulator rather than a free-water regulator.

ANP and BNP — sodium and water excretion

ANP is stored in atrial cells and released in response to atrial stretch. BNP is released from ventricular cells when diastolic pressures become abnormally high, including in heart failure. Both promote natriuresis and accompanying water excretion. When circulating volume declines, cardiac stretch and peptide release decline. The textbook notes that natriuretic peptides oppose aldosterone but are weaker.

Kidney perfusion and compensation

Urine volume also depends on adequate renal perfusion pressure and glomerular filtration rate (GFR); renal sympathetic nerves and prostaglandins additionally influence excretion. With excessive intake, kidneys generally produce more dilute urine. With insufficient intake or abnormal losses, thirst and water retention increase while urine volume falls. If these responses fail or are overwhelmed, fluid imbalance results.

Three-hormone memory aid: ADH conserves free water; aldosterone conserves sodium with water; ANP/BNP promote sodium and water excretion.
Textbook page 535

Fluid imbalances — Extracellular fluid volume deficit

Two types of fluid imbalances: saline/ECV imbalances affect the amount of isotonic extracellular fluid; water/concentration imbalances affect the concentration of body fluids. The two may coexist. An uncomplicated ECV deficit involves loss of sodium-containing fluid without a change in serum sodium concentration.

Animated explanation — ECV deficit

Vascular
Interstitial
Intracellular

ECV deficit: extracellular volume ↓, ICF unchanged ↔

Vascular ↓
Interstitial ↓
Intracellular ↔

Watch the red and blue fluid levels change. The green intracellular level remains constant.

Illustrative volume bars, not proportional anatomical measurements.

Mechanism: sodium and water are lost together in near-isotonic proportions → vascular and interstitial compartments shrink → ECF osmolality remains normal → no major osmotic water shift across cell membranes → ICF volume is unchanged.

Causes of extracellular fluid volume (ECV) deficit — Box 24.1

CategoryCauses
Gastrointestinal sodium-containing fluid lossVomiting (emesis); diarrhea including laxative overuse/abuse; gastric suction or intestinal decompression; fistula drainage.
Renal sodium-containing fluid lossAdrenal insufficiency; salt-wasting renal disorders; extensive diuretic use; bed rest.
OtherHemorrhage; massive diaphoresis; third-space sequestration; paracentesis and related procedures; burns.

Third spacing — fluid remains in the body but is unavailable

Sodium-containing fluid leaves the effective ECF
→
Rapid ascites or acute bowel obstruction
→
Effective circulating ECV falls

Because fluid accumulates in an inaccessible space rather than leaving the body, an ECV deficit may occur without a fall in total body weight.

Clinical manifestations

FindingMeaning
Sudden weight lossApproximately 1 kg of sudden weight loss equals 1 L of net fluid loss if measured accurately; third-spacing is an important exception.
Postural hypotension with concurrent tachycardiaA previously supine patient stands or sits with legs dependent; reduced vascular filling produces a blood-pressure fall with heart-rate rise.
Flat neck veins while supineMay collapse on inspiration because venous filling is reduced.
Prolonged small-vein filling and capillary refillReduced peripheral perfusion.
Lightheadedness, dizziness, syncopeReduced cerebral perfusion.
OliguriaIf renal compensation is intact, small volumes of concentrated, yellow urine are produced.

Additional signs when deficit develops gradually

  • Reduced skin turgor, with tenting when pinched over the sternum.
  • Dry oral mucosa between cheek and gum.
  • Hard stools; soft, sunken eyeballs; longitudinal tongue furrows.
  • Absence of tears and sweat.
  • In infants: sunken fontanel; neck-vein assessment is unreliable.
Clinical danger: Severe ECV deficit can progress to hypovolemic shock and requires effective fluid replacement.
Textbook page 536

Extracellular fluid volume excess

In uncomplicated ECV excess, the body contains too much isotonic sodium-containing ECF. Both vascular and interstitial volumes rise, while extracellular osmolality and intracellular cell volume remain normal.

Animated explanation — ECV excess

Vascular
Interstitial
Intracellular

ECV excess: extracellular volume ↑, ICF unchanged ↔

Vascular ↑
Interstitial ↑
Intracellular ↔

Watch the red and blue fluid levels change. The green intracellular level remains constant.

Illustrative volume bars, not proportional anatomical measurements.

Causes — Box 24.2 (complete)

CategoryCauses
Excessive IV isotonic fluidNormal saline (0.9% NaCl); Ringer infusion; lactated Ringer infusion.
Renal sodium and water retentionHyperaldosteronism; chronic heart failure; cirrhosis; acute glomerulonephritis; chronic end-stage renal disease; Cushing disease; corticosteroid therapy.

Why chronic heart failure can cause fluid excess

Reduced effective kidney perfusion
→
RAAS activation and aldosterone release
→
Na⁺ and water retention → ECV expansion

In heart failure, increased aldosterone is compensatory but may worsen fluid accumulation. The intermediate RAAS steps above are explanatory physiology expanding the textbook description.

Clinical manifestations

FindingExplanation
Sudden weight gainRapid sodium-containing water accumulation rather than overnight fat gain.
EdemaIncreased interstitial fluid.
Bounding pulseCirculatory overload.
Neck-vein distension while uprightIncreased venous filling and pressure.
Dependent lung crackles, dyspnea, orthopneaPulmonary congestion.
Frothy sputumCan occur with pulmonary edema.
Bulging fontanel in infantsInfant manifestation of excess fluid; neck veins cannot be assessed reliably in infants.
Salt-meal example: Weight may rise the day after a salty restaurant meal because salt and ingested water transiently expand ECV. The kidneys normally eliminate the excess. This helps explain low-sodium diets in conditions such as compensated heart failure.

Introduction to body fluid concentration

A water imbalance alters extracellular fluid concentration rather than simply the amount of isotonic saline. Banasik uses serum sodium as an indicator of blood osmolality: normal serum Na⁺ is 135–145 mEq/L (laboratory ranges may vary). Hyponatremia is below the lower limit; hypernatremia is above the upper limit. ECV and concentration disorders can coexist; hyponatremia continues on page 537.

ECV deficit versus ECV excess

FeatureDeficitExcess
ECV volume↓↑
ECF osmolalityNormal if uncomplicatedNormal if uncomplicated
ICF volumeUnchangedUnchanged
WeightSudden lossSudden gain
Neck veinsFlat supineDistended upright
Critical complicationHypovolemic shockPulmonary edema
Textbook page 537

Body fluid concentration disorders: hyponatremia and hypernatremia

Fluid volume and fluid concentration are distinct. An ECV deficit or excess describes how much isotonic saline is present. A fluid concentration disorder describes the amount of water relative to sodium in ECF. Serum sodium normally measures approximately 135–145 mEq/L. Concentration and volume problems may coexist.

ConditionSerum Na⁺Common osmotic effect
Hyponatremia<135 mEq/LHypotonic ECF; water enters cells
Normal135–145 mEq/LWater distribution balanced
Hypernatremia>145 mEq/LHypertonic ECF; water leaves cells

Qualification: Hyponatremia is usually hypotonic, but abnormal glucose or other effective osmoles can produce exceptions. Serum sodium measures a ratio, not total body sodium stores.

Hyponatremia — what causes it?

Hyponatremia means serum sodium falls below 135 mEq/L. Most often there is too much water relative to sodium. ECF becomes relatively dilute, and water shifts into cells by osmosis.

1. Gain of relatively more water than salt — dilutional hyponatremia

Excess ADH (such as SIADH), hypotonic fluid administration, psychogenic polydipsia, beer potomania, and other circumstances where water intake or retention exceeds renal excretory capacity. ADH acts on collecting ducts to increase water reabsorption through aquaporin-2 channels; retaining free water lowers serum sodium concentration.

2. Loss of relatively more salt than water — depletional hyponatremia

Examples include thiazide diuretics, renal salt wasting, or replacing losses from vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, or burns with plain water without replacing adequate sodium. Both mechanisms can coexist, as during exercise-associated hyponatremia.

Clinical example: SIADH

Small-cell lung carcinoma may produce ADH ectopically. Persistent ADH activity prevents appropriate excretion of free water, diluting sodium. Pain, nausea, stress, and certain medications may also increase ADH activity. The danger comes largely from water entering brain cells.

Figure 24.6 — Cell swelling in hyponatremia

Animated version — hypotonic ECF → water enters cell → swelling
Water shifts inward because ECF is relatively dilute.

Why the brain is vulnerable

Reduced extracellular osmolality → water enters neurons and glial cells → cellular swelling → cerebral edema and potentially increased intracranial pressure. Symptoms range from malaise, nausea, headache, and anorexia to confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma, and cerebral herniation.

Rate matters: Rapidly falling sodium is often more dangerous than a similar sodium concentration reached slowly, because brain cells have less time to adapt.

Hypernatremia — the opposite osmotic direction

Hypernatremia means serum Na⁺ exceeds 145 mEq/L. ECF contains too little water relative to sodium; it becomes hypertonic. Water moves out of cells, causing cellular shrinkage.

Gain of more sodium than water

Hypertonic saline administration, excessive sodium ingestion without adequate water, or concentrated tube feeds without sufficient water.

Loss of more water than sodium

Diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis, inadequate water intake, and excessive water losses without sufficient replacement.

Textbook page 538

Hypernatremia, clinical dehydration, and the onset of edema

Hypernatremia: clinical manifestations

When extracellular fluid is hypertonic, water leaves cells. Brain cells can shrink, leading to thirst, irritability or altered mental status, lethargy, seizures, and coma. Urinary output may be low when kidneys conserve water, but may be high when the cause is a renal water-loss disorder such as diabetes insipidus.

Contrast the two osmotic disorders

Hyponatremia: low effective ECF osmolality → water enters cells → swelling.
Hypernatremia: high ECF osmolality → water leaves cells → shrinkage. Both can produce severe neurologic dysfunction, but by opposite osmotic mechanisms.

Clinical dehydration: volume AND concentration

In this textbook, clinical dehydration describes the combination of ECV deficit and hypernatremia. There is insufficient extracellular fluid volume and not enough water relative to sodium. Gastrointestinal losses from vomiting or diarrhea, especially with inadequate water replacement, are common examples.

ECV deficit

Reduced vascular and interstitial fluid volume → tachycardia, postural hypotension, poor tissue perfusion, dry mucous membranes and potentially shock.

Hypernatremia

Increased ECF osmolality → water leaves cells → cell shrinkage and neurologic symptoms. Infants and older adults are especially vulnerable when they cannot adequately replace fluid.

Interstitial fluid volume: edema

Edema is excessive accumulation of fluid in interstitial tissues. It may accompany generalized ECV excess, or it may occur because capillary forces or lymphatic drainage are abnormal. Visible edema does not necessarily mean effective circulating blood volume is adequate.

MechanismWhy fluid accumulatesExample
↑ Capillary hydrostatic pressureMore fluid is pushed outward across capillariesVenous congestion, heart failure
↑ Interstitial oncotic pressure / capillary permeabilityMore proteins escape into interstitium and attract waterInflammation
Impaired lymphatic drainageProtein-rich interstitial fluid cannot be removed efficientlyLymph-node removal, obstruction, filariasis
↓ Plasma oncotic pressureLess albumin-dependent opposition to filtrationCirrhosis, significant protein loss

Mechanisms explained

Hydrostatic pressure: Venous congestion raises capillary pressure, encouraging filtration of water into interstitial tissue. Capillary permeability: In inflammation, plasma proteins can move into interstitium, raising its oncotic pressure and contributing to edema.

Lymphatic obstruction: Tumors, parasites, surgery, or fibrosis prevent normal clearance of interstitial proteins and fluid. Reduced plasma oncotic pressure: Low albumin weakens the force that opposes capillary filtration; this discussion continues on textbook page 539.

Clinical connection: ascites

Ascitic fluid is extracellular fluid accumulated in the peritoneal cavity. Its presence can coexist with reduced effective circulating volume, particularly in cirrhosis. Do not equate visible fluid accumulation with adequate perfusion of the arterial circulation.

Checkpoint

Explain why SIADH may cause cerebral edema; why diabetes insipidus may cause cellular shrinkage; how clinical dehydration combines a volume disorder with a concentration disorder; and why lymphatic obstruction creates edema even without generalized fluid overload.
